newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia prepares for refugee return to Serb region.
newsitem.headline: Croatia prepares for refugee return to Serb region.

text.p: The Croatian government started preparations on Monday for the return of around 40,000 Croatian refugees to the homes they fled in 1991 when rebel Serbs went to war with Croatia over its secession from Yugoslavia.
Around half of the 80,000 Croatians driven from the Serb-held region of Eastern Slavonia are expected to return by the end of the year, government officials said.
Their return will mean thousands of Serb families who have settled in the area will have to return to their own pre-war homes or leave Croatia altogether in order to vacate property.

"We have started preparations for the return of refugees in Eastern Slavonia today, and we hope to move the first ones in two weeks' time," Jure Radic, Minister for Reconstruction and Development, told a news conference.
He said the government wanted most to re-occupy former Croat homes by the start of the school year and in time for the autumn sowing season in the fertile area by the Danube river.

The region, occupied by Serb rebels and the Yugoslav army early in the 1991-95 war in former Yugoslavia, is at the moment controlled by a 5,000-strong United Nations mission which will begin winding down in the next few months.
The U.N. administration has to leave the area by January 15 next year, after which the Croatian government will regain full authority over it.

Eastern Slavonia is gradually reintegrating with the rest of Croatia. Serb number plates on cars are being exchanged for Croatian plates, local authorities taking shape and ethnic Serb residents taking Croatian citizenship papers.
More than 80,000 Croats fled or were expelled by Serb extremists and only a few dozen have been allowed to return during the 18 months of U.N. rule, Radic said.
The government on Monday dispatched teams to eight villages not so badly damaged in the war to check the status of housing for some 20,000 people, Radic said.
Zagreb has committed itself to rebuild flats for 10,000 people in the region's biggest town, Vukovar, which was flattened by the Yugoslav army during a three-month siege.
A further 10,000 people will return to villages positioned along the the former front line that were severely damaged in the conflict and are already being rebuilt.
Radic said the ministry would repair houses and move people back in groups to minimise security costs.
The return of Croatian refugees to Eastern Slavonia will set a precedent in ex-Yugoslavia, where war has left regions on all three sides -- Moslem, Croat and Serb -- ethnically "pure".

In tandem with the return of Croats to Eastern Slavonia, some 2,100 Serb families will leave the region and return to their homes in former rebel parts of Croatia which they fled in 1995 when the areas were recaptured by the Croatian army.
Another 2,400 Serb families who want to leave Croatia altogether will be compensated for their property through the State Real Estate Agency, according to Radic.
